title: Predicting Protein Interactions
markdown:
## What this covers

This chapter is the transcript-free record of lecture 14 in MIT's 7.091J (*Foundations of
Computational and Systems Biology*), the point in the course where prediction work turns from a
single protein's structure to how two or more proteins interact. Only the slide deck survived
conversion, and much of it did not convert to text, so what follows is deliberately short: it
states the one idea the extracted text actually supports, and says plainly what the chapter cannot
reconstruct. It assumes the previous lecture's material on predicting protein structure.

## From structure to interaction

The lecture opens by placing itself in the course's arc, given as a run of six lectures:

- L12 — Introduction to Protein Structure; Structure Comparison and Classification
- L13 — Predicting protein structure
- L14 — Predicting protein interactions
- L15 — Gene Regulatory Networks
- L16 — Protein Interaction Networks
- L17 — Computable Network Models

The recap slide states the pivot directly: last time, protein structure; now, protein interactions.
The only content carried over from the previous lecture in this deck is a single citation, credited
on the recap slide: Lindorff-Larsen, Piana, et al., "How Fast-Folding Proteins Fold," *Science* 334,
no. 6055 (2011): 517-20. The slide deck does not say what point the citation illustrated; whatever
argument it supported belongs to lecture 13, not this one.

## Graphical structure as a statement of belief

The one idea stated outright in the recovered text is about how to represent a system of
interacting proteins for prediction: as a graph, where which nodes are connected encodes a belief
about which parts of the system affect which others. The slide gives two ways such a graph can be
obtained:

- **decided in advance**, from existing knowledge of the system — the modeler fixes which
  interactions the graph will contain before looking at data, based on what is already known
  biologically; or
- **learned from the data** — the graph's structure itself is treated as unknown and is inferred
  from observations, rather than assumed.

The slide does not go further than this framing in the material that survived conversion: no
worked example, no comparison of the two approaches, and no statement of which one the rest of the
lecture pursues. Whatever method or dataset it was building toward lives in the lecture's figures,
not in the extracted text.

## What this chapter cannot cover

The original PDF is image-heavy: the conversion recovered file names for over eighty figures spread
across roughly the first two-thirds of a much longer deck, but not one figure caption or any of the
diagram content itself, and no transcript was supplied to narrate them. That is almost certainly
where the bulk of the lecture's actual content sits — most plausibly the specific
interaction-prediction methods the "Graphical Structure Expresses our Beliefs" slide was
introducing, and any worked comparison of a hand-specified graph against a learned one. None of it
can be honestly reconstructed from what is here, so this chapter stops at the one general principle
the surviving text supports rather than guessing at the material behind it.

## Sources

- Slides: `14-slides.md` (MIT OCW 7.091J, *Foundations of Computational and Systems Biology*,
  Spring 2014), lecture 14, "Predicting protein interactions" — CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, converted from a
  PDF with no text layer by a model reading the pages, fidelity marked "reconstructed." Used for
  the lecture's table of contents, the structure-to-interactions recap, the citation to
  Lindorff-Larsen et al. (2011), and the "Graphical Structure Expresses our Beliefs" slide.
- No transcript, instructor notes, or problem set were supplied for this lecture.
- Referred to but not contained in the supplied material: Lindorff-Larsen, Kresten, Stefano Piana,
  et al., "How Fast-folding Proteins Fold," *Science* 334, no. 6055 (2011): 517-20; and the roughly
  eighty uncaptioned figures listed in the source markdown's Figures section, which carry most of
  this lecture's actual content on predicting protein interactions.
